title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 860–862 (Night 198, continuing nights-197), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 198 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. The prince's first words after his long silence, asking that the young stranger sit beside him, come just in time: the sultan, his father, had secretly resolved to have Marzawān beheaded, and now he rejoices, seats Marzawān by his son, and asks where he comes from — from the Inner Islands, Marzawān says, the lands of King al-Ghayūr, lord of the islands, the seas and the seven palaces. Unnoticed by the court, Marzawān whispers to the prince to take heart: the lady for whom he has wasted away is in a worse plight for his sake, for he hid his love and grew weak, while she showed hers and was called mad, and now lies imprisoned with an iron chain about her neck; but the cure of them both will come at Marzawān's hand. Qamar al-Zamān's spirit returns; he signs to be sat up, the king all but flies for joy, shakes out the kerchief to dismiss his emirs and viziers, perfumes the palace with saffron and has the city decorated. Marzawān bids the prince eat with him, and he does; the king tells the queen and the palace, the drums of good tidings are beaten, the city rejoices, and the king spends the night with the two young men in his gladness. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّامِنَةُ وَالتِّسْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāminatu wa-al-tisʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the eighth and the ninety after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and ninety-eighth night,
sentences.n: al-thāmina, “the eighth”, feminine to agree with layla; then wa-al-tisʿūna, “and the ninety”, and baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”, as in the nights before. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ مَرْزَوَانَ قَالَ لِوَالِدِهِ يَا أَبِي خَلِّ هٰذَا الشَّابَّ يَأْتِي وَيَجْلِسُ فِي جَانِبِي
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Marzawāna qāla li-wālidihi yā abī khalli hādhā al-shābba yaʾtī wa-yajlisu fī jānibī
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Marzawān said to-his-father: O my-father, let this the-young-man come and-sit at my-side.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Marzawān said to his father, “Father, let this young man come and sit beside me.”
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the last words of the night before, but in the retelling the speaker has changed: it was Qamar al-Zamān who spoke these words to his own father, the sultan, and Marzawān is the young man he asks for. The slip is the text’s own; it is kept, and the English follows the Arabic. The words differ a little too: last night the prince said daʿ, “let”, and ilā jānibī; here it is khalli, imperative of khallā, Form II, “to leave, let”, the everyday word, and fī jānibī, “at my side”. As before, the verbs after the imperative are plain imperfects, yaʾtī wa-yajlisu, not the Classical jussive. li-wālidihi: li- marks the one spoken to. The hamza of يأتي is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ السُّلْطَانُ مِنْ وَلَدِهِ قَمَرِالزَّمَانِ ذٰلِكَ فَرِحَ فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا بَعْدَ أَنْ كَانَ قَلْبُهُ تَغَيَّرَ مِنْ جِهَةِ مَرْزَوَانَ وَأَضْمَرَ فِي نَفْسِهِ أَنَّهُ لَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَرْمِىَ رَقَبَتَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-sulṭānu min waladihi Qamari al-Zamāni dhālika fariḥa faraḥan shadīdan baʿda an kāna qalbuhu taghayyara min jihati Marzawāna wa-aḍmara fī nafsihi annahu lā budda an yarmiya raqabatahu
sentences.l: So-when heard the-sultan from his-son Qamar al-Zamān that, he-rejoiced (with) a-rejoicing intense, after that had his-heart changed from (the) direction (of) Marzawān, and-he-had-concealed in himself that-he, no escape, that he-cast-off his-neck.
sentences.i: When the sultan heard this from his son Qamar al-Zamān, he rejoiced greatly; for his heart had turned against Marzawān, and he had resolved in secret that he must have his head struck off.
sentences.n: fariḥa faraḥan shadīdan, “he rejoiced a great rejoicing”: the verb with its own verbal noun as object, the cognate accusative, strengthened by an adjective. baʿda an kāna … taghayyara, “after his heart had changed”: kāna with a perfect gives the pluperfect. min jihati, “on the side of, regarding”. aḍmara fī nafsihi, “he hid in himself”, to resolve on something without saying it. lā budda an, “there is no escape from …”, “must”. ramā raqabatahu, “to throw off his neck”, is to behead; the text does not say why; the vizier had warned Marzawān that the sultan’s heart was full of rage, and the stranger had gone straight up to the prince, stared at him and recited verses. The prince’s first words save Marzawān’s life. The print spells the verb with ى, يرمى, for يرمي; it is kept, and read yarmiya, subjunctive after an. The print sets قمرالزمان as one word; the spacing is kept.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ وَلَدَهُ تَكَلَّمَ زَالَ مَابِهِ وَنَهَضَ قَائِمًا وَجَذَبَ الْغُلَامَ مَرْزَوَانَ وَأَجْلَسَهُ بِجَانِبِ قَمَرِالزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa waladahu takallama zāla mā bihi wa-nahaḍa qāʾiman wa-jadhaba al-ghulāma Marzawāna wa-ajlasahu bi-jānibi Qamari al-Zamāni
sentences.l: So-when he-heard his-son (he) spoke, ceased what (was) in-him, and-he-rose standing, and-drew the-youth Marzawān and-seated-him at-(the)-side (of) Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: When he heard his son speak, what had weighed on him fell away; he rose to his feet, drew the youth Marzawān forward, and seated him beside Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.n: samiʿa waladahu takallama, “he heard his son, he spoke”: the second verb follows the object directly, with no an, as spoken Arabic does it: “heard his son speak”. zāla mā bihi, “what was in him ceased”: his grief and his anger both. The print sets ما به as one word, مابه; the spacing is kept. nahaḍa qāʾiman, “he rose up standing”, a common pairing. ajlasa, Form IV, “to seat (someone)”, the causative of jalasa. bi-jānibi, “at the side of”: bi- marks place. The ئ of قائما is printed, and قمرالزمان is again set as one word.

sentences.t: وَأَقْبَلَ الْمَلِكُ عَلَى مَرْزَوَانَ وَقَالَ لَهُ الْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ عَلَى سَلَامَتِكَ فَقَالَ لَهُ سَلَّمَ اللّٰهُ لَكَ وَلَدَكَ وَدَعَا لِلْمَلِكِ
sentences.tr: wa-aqbala al-maliku ʿalā Marzawāna wa-qāla lahu al-ḥamdu li-llāhi ʿalā salāmatika fa-qāla lahu sallama Allāhu laka waladaka wa-daʿā li-al-maliki
sentences.l: And-turned the-king toward Marzawān and-said to-him: The praise (belongs) to-God for your-safety. And-he-said to-him: May-keep-safe God for-you your-son; and-he-prayed for-the-king.
sentences.i: The king turned to Marzawān and said to him, “Praise be to God for your safe arrival.” Marzawān answered, “May God keep your son safe for you,” and called down blessings on the king.
sentences.n: aqbala ʿalā, “to turn toward, give one’s attention to”. al-ḥamdu li-llāhi ʿalā salāmatika, “praise be to God for your safety”, is the greeting given to a traveller who has come through safely, and Marzawān answers on the same root, s-l-m: sallama Allāhu laka waladaka, “may God keep your son safe for you”, a wish put in the perfect, as blessings are. li-llāhi: li-, “to, belonging to”. laka is li- with the suffix -ka: “for you”, the one who benefits. daʿā li-, “to pray for (someone)”: li- marks the one prayed for.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ مِنْ أَيِّ الْبِلَادِ أَنْتَ قَالَ مِنَ الْجَزَائِرِ الْجَوَّانِيَّةِ مِنْ بِلَادِ الْمَلِكِ الْغَيُورِ صَاحِبِ الْجَزَائِرِ وَالْبُحُورِ وَالسَّبْعَةِ قُصُورٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-maliku min ayyi al-bilādi anta qāla mina al-jazāʾiri al-jawwāniyyati min bilādi al-maliki al-Ghayūri ṣāḥibi al-jazāʾiri wa-al-buḥūri wa-al-sabʿati quṣūrin
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-king: From which (of) the-lands (are) you? He-said: From the-islands the-inner, from (the) lands (of) the-king al-Ghayūr, lord (of) the-islands and-the-seas and-the-seven palaces.
sentences.i: Then the king asked him, “From what country are you?” He said, “From the Inner Islands, from the lands of King al-Ghayūr, lord of the islands and the seas and the seven palaces.”
sentences.n: al-jazāʾir al-jawwāniyya, “the Inner Islands”: jawwānī, “inner, inside”, is a word of the spoken language. al-Ghayūr, “the Jealous”, is the father of the princess Budūr, and “lord of the islands and the seas and the seven palaces” is his title in the tale; al-buḥūr and quṣūr chime with al-Ghayūr itself, a small run of rhyme in -ūr. wa-al-sabʿati quṣūrin, “and the seven palaces”: Classical Arabic would put the numeral in construct without an article, sabʿati quṣūrin, or say al-quṣūri al-sabʿati; the text gives the numeral the article and leaves the counted noun bare, as Middle Arabic often does. It is kept as printed. ayyi, “which”, takes the noun after it in the genitive; its shadda is printed, as is the ئ of الجزائر.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ عَسَى أَنْ يَكُونَ قُدُومُكَ مُبَارَكًا عَلَى وَلَدِي وَيُنَجِّيَهُ اللّٰهُ مِمَّا هُوَ فِيهِ فَقَالَ إِنْ شَاءَ اللّٰهُ تَعَالَى مَا يَكُونُ إِلَّا الْخَيْرُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-maliku Shahramānu ʿasā an yakūna qudūmuka mubārakan ʿalā waladī wa-yunajjiyahu Allāhu mimmā huwa fīhi fa-qāla in shāʾa Allāhu taʿālā mā yakūnu illā al-khayru
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-king Shahramān: Perhaps that may-be your-coming blessed upon my-son, and-may-save-him God from-what he (is) in-it. And-he-said: If willed God (the) Exalted, not will-be except the-good.
sentences.i: King Shahramān said to him, “May your coming bring a blessing on my son, and may God deliver him from what he suffers.” He said, “God willing, nothing will come of it but good.”
sentences.n: Shahramān is Qamar al-Zamān’s father, the sultan of the sentences before. ʿasā an, “it may be that”, the usual way to voice a hope; yakūna and yunajjiyahu are both subjunctive after an. najjā, Form II, “to rescue, deliver”. mimmā is min mā, “from what”; mimmā huwa fīhi, “from what he is in”, his illness. in shāʾa Allāhu taʿālā, “if God, (who is) exalted, wills”. mā yakūnu illā al-khayru, “there will be nothing but good”: mā with the imperfect for a future negation is the spoken usage; Classical prose would prefer lā or lan. The hamza of شاء is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ مَرْزَوَانَ أَقْبَلَ عَلَى قَمَرِالزَّمَانِ وَقَالَ لَهُ فِي أُذُنِهِ فِي غَفْلَةِ الْمَلِكِ وَأَهْلِ الدَّوْلَةِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Marzawāna aqbala ʿalā Qamari al-Zamāni wa-qāla lahu fī udhunihi fī ghaflati al-maliki wa-ahli al-dawlati
sentences.l: Then indeed Marzawān turned toward Qamar al-Zamān and-said to-him in his-ear, in (the) heedlessness (of) the-king and-(the)-people (of) the-state:
sentences.i: Then Marzawān turned to Qamar al-Zamān and, while the king and his court were not attending, whispered in his ear,
sentences.n: thumma inna followed by a subject and a perfect verb, “then (it was so that) Marzawān turned”, is the text’s usual way of moving the story on; inna adds no emphasis here. fī ghaflati, “in the heedlessness of”, “unnoticed by”. ahl al-dawla, “the people of the state”, the courtiers about the king. The print again sets قمرالزمان solid.

sentences.t: يَا سَيِّدِي شُدَّ رُوحَكَ وَقَوِّ قَلْبَكَ وَقَرَّعَيْنَكَ
sentences.tr: yā sayyidī shudda rūḥaka wa-qawwi qalbaka wa-qarra ʿaynaka
sentences.l: O my-lord, bind-firm your-spirit, and-strengthen your-heart, and-be-cool (in) your-eye,
sentences.i: “My lord, take heart, be strong, and let your eyes be at rest;
sentences.n: Three imperatives in a row. shudd rūḥaka, “tie your spirit tight”, “brace yourself”, a spoken idiom. qawwi, imperative of qawwā, Form II, “to strengthen”; the final yā of the root drops in the imperative. qarra ʿaynaka, “be cool of eye”: a cool eye is one at rest and comforted, as against the hot eye of weeping; the usual phrase is qarra ʿaynan or qarrat ʿaynuka, “may your eye be cool”, and here the eye takes the possessive. The print sets the two words solid, قرّعينك, and the spacing is kept. The shaddas of سيّدي, شدّ, قوّ and قرّعينك are printed.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّ الَّتِي صِرْتَ مِنْ أَجْلِهَا هٰكَذَا لَا تَسْأَلْ عَمَّا هِيَ فِيهِ مِنْ أَجْلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-inna allatī ṣirta min ajlihā hākadhā lā tasʾal ʿammā hiya fīhi min ajlika
sentences.l: for indeed she-who you-have-become for her-sake thus — do-not ask about-what she (is) in-it for your-sake.
sentences.i: for she on whose account you have come to this — do not even ask what she suffers on yours.
sentences.n: allatī, “she who”, the princess Budūr, still not named to him. ṣirta hākadhā, “you have become thus”: ṣāra, “to become”. min ajli, “for the sake of, because of”. The sentence begins with inna allatī … and then breaks off into a command: lā tasʾal ʿammā hiya fīhi, “do not ask about what she is in”, that is, it is beyond telling. tasʾal is jussive after lā of prohibition; ʿammā is ʿan mā, “about what”. The hamza of تسأل is printed.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنَّكَ كَتَمْتَ أَمْرَكَ فَضَعُفْتَ وَأَمَّا هِيَ فَإِنَّهَا أَظْهَرَتْ أَمْرَهَا فَقَالُوا إِنَّهَا جُنَّتْ
sentences.tr: wa-lākinnaka katamta amraka fa-ḍaʿufta wa-ammā hiya fa-innahā aẓharat amrahā fa-qālū innahā junnat
sentences.l: But-you concealed your-affair, so-you-grew-weak; and-as-for her, indeed-she made-plain her-affair, so-they-said that-she was-possessed.
sentences.i: But you kept your secret, and so you wasted away; she made hers known, and so they said she was mad.
sentences.n: The two lovers are set against each other: katamta, “you concealed”, and aẓharat, “she revealed”, each with amr, “affair, case”. ammā … fa-, “as for … (then)”, the usual frame for a contrast. junnat, passive of janna, “she was struck by the jinn”, is the ordinary word for going mad. After qālū, “they said”, the particle is inna with kasra, as after every verb of saying. The shadda of جنّت is printed.

sentences.t: وَهِيَ الْآنَ مَسْجُونَةٌ وَفِي رَقَبَتِهَا سِلْسِلَةٌ مِنَ الْحَدِيدِ وَهِيَ فِي أَسْوَ حَالٍ
sentences.tr: wa-hiya al-āna masjūnatun wa-fī raqabatihā silsilatun mina al-ḥadīdi wa-hiya fī aswa ḥālin
sentences.l: And-she (is) now imprisoned, and-on her-neck (is) a-chain of the-iron, and-she (is) in (the) worst (of) state.
sentences.i: Now she is shut away with an iron chain about her neck, in the worst of plights.
sentences.n: Three nominal clauses, each opened by wa-: wa-hiya … wa-fī raqabatihā … wa-hiya, “and she … and on her neck … and she”. The mad were chained so in the hospitals of the time. aswa ḥālin, “the worst of states”: the print has اسو for أسوأ, the word’s final hamza dropped as in speech; it is kept, and read as spelt, where Classical Arabic has aswaʾi ḥālin. An elative such as aswaʾ before an indefinite noun means “the worst of”. The madda of الآن is printed.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ شَاءَ اللّٰهُ تَعَالَى يَكُونُ دَوَاؤُكُمَا عَلَيٰ يَدِي
sentences.tr: wa-in shāʾa Allāhu taʿālā yakūnu dawāʾukumā ʿalā yadī
sentences.l: And-if willed God (the) Exalted, will-be the-cure-of-you-two at my-hand.
sentences.i: But, God willing, the cure of you both will come at my hand.”
sentences.n: dawāʾukumā, “the remedy of you two”: -kumā is the dual “your”, for the prince and the princess together. ʿalā yadī, “at my hand”, “through me”. The formula in shāʾa Allāh stands apart from the sentence, so the verb after it is a plain imperfect, yakūnu, not a conditional jussive. The print spells ʿalā with dotted yā, علي, for على; it is kept, and read ʿalā. The damma of دواؤُكما, and its ؤ, are printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ قَمَرُالزَّمَانِ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ رُدَّتْ رُوحُهُ إِلَيْهِ وَاشْتَدَّ قَلْبُهُ وَحَصَلَ عِنْدَهُ نَشَاطٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Qamaru al-Zamāni hādhā al-kalāma ruddat rūḥuhu ilayhi wa-ishtadda qalbuhu wa-ḥaṣala ʿindahu nashāṭun
sentences.l: So-when heard Qamar al-Zamān this the-speech, was-returned his-spirit to-him, and-grew-strong his-heart, and-came-about with-him liveliness.
sentences.i: When Qamar al-Zamān heard these words, his spirit came back to him, his heart grew strong, and new vigour stirred in him.
sentences.n: ruddat, passive of radda, “to give back”: “his soul was returned to him”. rūḥ, “spirit”, is usually feminine, hence ruddat. ishtadda, Form VIII, “to become firm, strong”. ḥaṣala ʿindahu, “there came about with him”: what one comes to feel is said to “arise with” one. nashāṭ, “energy, liveliness”. Again قمرالزمان is printed solid.

sentences.t: وَأَشَارَ إِلَى أَبِيهِ أَنْ يُجْلِسَهُ فَكَادَ الْمَلِكُ أَنْ يَطِيرَ مِنَ الْفَرَحِ وَنَهَضَ إِلَى وَلَدِهِ وَأَجْلَسَهُ فَجَلَسَ قَمَرُالزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-ashāra ilā abīhi an yujlisahu fa-kāda al-maliku an yaṭīra mina al-faraḥi wa-nahaḍa ilā waladihi wa-ajlasahu fa-jalasa Qamaru al-Zamāni
sentences.l: And-he-signed to his-father that he-seat-him (up); so-almost the-king (did) that he-fly from the-joy, and-he-rose to his-son and-seated-him, and-sat Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: He made a sign to his father to sit him up, and the king all but flew for joy; he went to his son and raised him, and Qamar al-Zamān sat up.
sentences.n: ashāra ilā … an, “to make a sign to (someone) that”, that is, to ask by gesture. yujlisahu, Form IV, “to seat him”, here to lift a man lying in bed into a sitting position. kāda, “to be on the point of”, is followed in Classical prose mostly by a bare imperfect, kāda yaṭīru; kāda an yaṭīra, with an, also occurs and is the text’s choice here. min al-faraḥ, “from joy”: min gives the cause. The print sets قمرالزمان solid.

sentences.t: فَنَفَضَ الْمَلِكُ الْمِنْدِيلَ مِنْ خَوْفِهِ عَلَى وَلَدِهِ فَانْصَرَفَتْ جَمِيعُ الْأُمَرَاءِ وَالْوُزَرَاءِ وَوَضَعَ لَهُ مِخَدَّتَيْنِ فَجَلَسَ مُتَّكِئًا
sentences.tr: fa-nafaḍa al-maliku al-mindīla min khawfihi ʿalā waladihi fa-inṣarafat jamīʿu al-umarāʾi wa-al-wuzarāʾi wa-waḍaʿa lahu mikhaddatayni fa-jalasa muttakiʾan
sentences.l: And-shook-out the-king the-kerchief, from his-fear for his-son, so-departed all (of) the-emirs and-the-viziers; and-he-placed for-him two-cushions, and-he-sat reclining.
sentences.i: Then the king, fearing for his son, shook out the kerchief, and all the emirs and viziers withdrew. He set two cushions for him, and the prince sat reclining against them.
sentences.n: nafaḍa al-mindīl, “he shook out the kerchief”: the king’s signal that the audience is over and the court should leave; he dismisses them so that the crowd will not tire his son. khawf ʿalā, “fear for (someone)”. inṣarafat, Form VII, “to go away”; it is feminine because a plural of persons, here jamīʿ al-umarāʾ, may take a feminine singular verb. mikhaddatayni, “two cushions”, the dual of mikhadda, “a pillow for the cheek”. muttakiʾan, “reclining”, the participle of ittakaʾa, Form VIII, a clause of state. The hamzas of الامراء, الوزراء and متكئا are printed.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَ الْمَلِكُ أَنْ يُطَيَّبَ الْقَصْرُ بِالزَّعْفَرَانِ ثُمَّ أَمَرَ بِزِينَةِ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-amara al-maliku an yuṭayyaba al-qaṣru bi-al-zaʿfarāni thumma amara bi-zīnati al-madīnati
sentences.l: And-commanded the-king that be-perfumed the-palace with-the-saffron; then he-commanded the-adorning (of) the-city.
sentences.i: The king ordered the palace to be perfumed with saffron, and then commanded that the city be decked out.
sentences.n: yuṭayyaba, passive subjunctive of ṭayyaba, Form II, “to scent, perfume”; bi-al-zaʿfarān, “with saffron”: bi- marks the means. amara bi-, “to order (something)”: the verb takes the thing ordered with bi-. zīna, “adornment”: lamps, hangings and silks put up in the streets for a public rejoicing.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لِمَرْزَوَانَ وَاللّٰهِ يَا وَلَدِي إِنَّ طَلْعَتَكَ سَعِيدَةٌ مُبَارَكَةٌ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla li-Marzawāna wa-Allāhi yā waladī inna ṭalʿataka saʿīdatun mubārakatun
sentences.l: And-he-said to-Marzawān: By-God, O my-son, indeed your-appearing (is) fortunate, blessed.
sentences.i: And he said to Marzawān, “By God, my son, your coming has brought good fortune and blessing.”
sentences.n: wa-Allāhi, “by God”: the wāw of oath, which takes the genitive. yā waladī, “my son”, said in affection to a young man not his own. ṭalʿa, “appearance, the face one shows on arriving”: a man whose ṭalʿa is saʿīda brings luck with him. li-Marzawāna: li- marks the one spoken to.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَكْرَمَهُ غَايَةَ الْإِكْرَامِ وَطَلَبَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ الطَّعَامَ فَقَدَّمُوهُ لَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma akramahu ghāyata al-ikrāmi wa-ṭalaba lahu al-maliku al-ṭaʿāma fa-qaddamūhu lahu
sentences.l: Then he-honoured-him (to the) utmost (of) the-honouring, and-called for-him the-king the-food, and-they-brought-it-forward to-him.
sentences.i: Then he showed him every honour, and the king called for food for him, and they set it before him.
sentences.n: akramahu ghāyata al-ikrāmi, “he honoured him the limit of honouring”: the verbal noun ikrām in an accusative phrase says how far. lahu, “for him”, twice: li- marks the one the food is for. Who “he” is is left open; what follows shows that the meal is set where both young men can eat.

sentences.t: فَتَقَدَّمَ مَرْزَوَانُ وَقَالَ لِقَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ تَقَدَّمْ كُلْ مَعِي فَطَاوَعَهُ وَتَقَدَّمَ وَأَكَلَ مَعَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-taqaddama Marzawānu wa-qāla li-Qamari al-Zamāni taqaddam kul maʿī fa-ṭāwaʿahu wa-taqaddama wa-akala maʿahu
sentences.l: And-came-forward Marzawān and-said to-Qamar al-Zamān: Come-forward, eat with-me. And-he-obeyed-him, and-came-forward, and-ate with-him.
sentences.i: Marzawān drew up to the food and said to Qamar al-Zamān, “Come, eat with me.” He did as he was told, drew up, and ate with him.
sentences.n: The print has نطاوعه, a misprint for فطاوعه, corrected here. ṭāwaʿa, Form III, “to comply with, do as (someone) asks”. taqaddama, Form V, “to come forward”, here to the dish. taqaddam kul maʿī, “come forward, eat with me”: two imperatives side by side with no “and”, as in speech; kul is the short imperative of akala, “to eat”. li-Qamari: li- marks the one spoken to; here the print sets قمر الزمان as two words. The shadda of the second and third تقدّم is printed.

sentences.t: كُلُّ هٰذَا وَالْمَلِكُ يَدْعُو لِمَرْزَوَانَ وَيَقُولُ مَا أَحْسَنَ قُدُومَكَ يَا وَلَدِي
sentences.tr: kullu hādhā wa-al-maliku yadʿū li-Marzawāna wa-yaqūlu mā aḥsana qudūmaka yā waladī
sentences.l: All this, and-the-king praying for-Marzawān and-saying: How good (is) your-coming, O my-son!
sentences.i: All the while the king was calling down blessings on Marzawān and saying, “How welcome your coming is, my son!”
sentences.n: kullu hādhā wa-, “all this, and …”: the narrator’s way of saying “all the while”; the wa- clause is one of state. yadʿū li-, “to pray for”: li- marks the one prayed for. mā aḥsana qudūmaka, “how good your coming is!”: mā with the verb of wonder aḥsana, and the thing admired in the accusative.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى وَالِدُهُ أَكْلَ وَلَدِهِ زَادَ بِهِ الْفَرَحُ وَالسُّرُورُ وَخَرَجَ مِنْ وَقْتِهِ وَأَخْبَرَ أُمَّهُ وَأَهْلَ الْقَصْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā wāliduhu akla waladihi zāda bihi al-faraḥu wa-al-surūru wa-kharaja min waqtihi wa-akhbara ummahu wa-ahla al-qaṣri
sentences.l: So-when saw his-father (the) eating (of) his-son, increased in-him the-joy and-the-gladness, and-he-went-out from his-time and-informed his-mother and-(the)-people (of) the-palace.
sentences.i: When the father saw his son eat, his joy and gladness overflowed; he went out at once and told the prince’s mother and the people of the palace.
sentences.n: The pronouns look from the son’s side: wāliduhu, “his father”, and ummahu, “his mother”, are the prince’s, though it is the father who sees and goes out. akla waladihi, “the eating of his son”, takes akl as a verbal noun; it could also be read as a clause, akala waladuhu, “(that) his son ate”. zāda bihi, “increased in him”: bi- here marks the one affected. min waqtihi, “from his time”, “at once”. The hamza of رأى is printed.

sentences.t: فَضُرِبَتِ الْبَشَائِرُ فِى الْقَصْرِ لِسَلَامَةِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَنَادَى الْمَلِكُ بِالزِّينَةِ فَزُيِّنَتِ الْمَدِينَةُ وَفَرِحَتِ النَّاسُ وَكَانَ يَوْمًا عَظِيمًا
sentences.tr: fa-ḍuribati al-bashāʾiru fī al-qaṣri li-salāmati Qamari al-Zamāni wa-nādā al-maliku bi-al-zīnati fa-zuyyinati al-madīnatu wa-fariḥati al-nāsu wa-kāna yawman ʿaẓīman
sentences.l: And-were-beaten the-glad-tidings in the-palace for-(the)-safety (of) Qamar al-Zamān, and-proclaimed the-king the-adorning, so-was-adorned the-city, and-rejoiced the-people, and-it-was a-day great.
sentences.i: Then the drums of good tidings were beaten in the palace for Qamar al-Zamān’s recovery; the king had the decorating proclaimed, the city was decked out, the people rejoiced, and it was a great day.
sentences.n: ḍuribat al-bashāʾir, “the glad tidings were beaten”: the drums and kettledrums that announce good news, called by the news they bring. li-salāmati, “for the safety of”: li- gives the reason. nādā bi-, “to proclaim (something)”, the thing cried abroad taking bi-. zuyyinat, passive of zayyana, Form II, “to adorn”; its shadda is printed. fariḥat al-nāsu, “the people rejoiced”, with a feminine verb, as the text often treats al-nās as a feminine collective. The print writes fī as فى and sets قمر الزمان as two words; both are kept. The ئ of البشائر is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ مَرْزَوَانَ بَاتَ تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ عِنْدَ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَبَاتَ الْمَلِكُ عِنْدَهُمَا مِنْ فَرْحَتِهِ وَهُوَ مَسْرُورٌ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Marzawāna bāta tilka al-laylata ʿinda Qamari al-Zamāni wa-bāta al-maliku ʿindahumā min farḥatihi wa-huwa masrūrun
sentences.l: Then indeed Marzawān spent-the-night that the-night with Qamar al-Zamān, and-spent-the-night the-king with-them-two from his-joy, and-he (was) glad.
sentences.i: Marzawān spent that night with Qamar al-Zamān, and the king, for very joy, spent it with the two of them, happy at heart.
sentences.n: thumma inna again moves the story on. bāta, “to pass the night”; tilka al-laylata, “that night”, accusative of time. ʿindahumā, “with the two of them”, dual. farḥa, “a joy”, the single-instance noun of faraḥ, much used in speech; min gives the cause. wa-huwa masrūrun, “and he glad”, a clause of state.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night; this time the print sets the name as one word, شهرزاد. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
